Los Angeles, 2004–2026: technical appendix

Author

Boris Shor

The substantive report presents the expanded pooled scale. The original recent-only appendix remains available separately.

Historical source construction

Code/52_collect_la_history.py inventories the City Clerk’s annual journal folders, caches the original PDFs and HTML, and records source URLs and capture metadata under Data/LosAngeles/history/. HTML decoding handles both UTF-8 and older Windows encodings. Text-native PDFs were checked with the text-PDF extraction workflow; bulk parser input uses layout-preserving pdftotext. Image-only or unreadable content is not silently treated as zero votes.

Code/53_parse_la_history.py uses the meeting date printed inside the journal, not its upload date or URL filename. The attendance list supplies the member universe. A person initially absent may cast a later vote; the initial present/absent split is not carried forward to individual actions. A named vacancy is never assigned a legislator.

Named nays, absences and nonbinary responses are retained separately. Remaining members are assigned yea only if their count reproduces the printed yea tally and the categories account for the named meeting roster. Conflicting cells, unresolved names and unreconciled tallies are excluded. When a printed attendance count is a typographical mismatch with its names, the names supply the universe and each action’s tally must still reconcile; such attendance discrepancies are flagged in the document audit.

For older journals, repeated references to one numbered roll call are collapsed when their response vectors agree; conflicting versions are excluded. The newer format lacks roll-call numbers, so distinct recorded outcomes remain separate. Exact duplicate documents are removed. No deduplication merely on identical voting patterns is applied, and there is no repeated-pattern sensitivity fit.

The historical backfill ends before February 16, 2021, when the preserved published export begins. Only successfully reconciled contested historical actions enter the pooled matrix. The recent component is the already constructed 624-action matrix, so its cells and action keys are preserved exactly; the two sources cannot overlap in date. The recent raw-action denominator is not added to historical outcome-header counts as if the two were comparable measures of independent decisions.

The issue table includes exclusions encountered during capture and parsing, not a census of missing historical votes. Documents outside the requested historical date boundary are also not used. Some rejected actions are unanimous and would not qualify anyway. Neither parser agreement with printed totals nor a bounded source sample constitutes corpus-wide accuracy certification.

Distribution and polarization plots

Density plots summarize posterior mean positions with equal weight per member, not posterior draws or vote counts. A common Gaussian bandwidth (bw.nrd0 of the 45 pooled means) is used across councils. Curves are evaluated within each group’s observed range, tapered linearly to zero over one bandwidth at its edges and renormalized to area one. This is a descriptive smoothing choice, not evidence of additional members outside the observed range; rug marks show the actual points. Council-wide polarization uses the interquartile range and 90th-minus-10th percentile spread. Party separation is the Republican median minus the Democratic median, excluding Zine from static party groups. Counts and derived quantities are in Results/LosAngeles-expanded/polarization.csv; no refit is involved.

Estimation in R

The one-dimensional probit model is

Pr⁡(yij=1)=Φ(βjxi−αj).\Pr(y_{ij}=1)=\Phi(\beta_j x_i-\alpha_j).

The member position is xix_i; each roll call has a discrimination βj\beta_j and difficulty αj\alpha_j. pscl::ideal() uses its default normal priors and normalization. Missing cells contribute no vote likelihood. Sign is oriented to a vote-derived singular vector with John Lee positive.

Code/54_fit_la_expanded.r runs exactly two independent-seed chains. Democratic initial positions are −1, Republican +1, and the switcher starts at 0. These are starting values, not party priors or fixed coordinates. Greuel and Park start as Democrats because their earlier Republican affiliations preceded their observed council votes. Organizational endorsements do not enter the model.

chains iterations burnin thin max_rhat min_ess chain_mean_correlation
2 605000 205000 200 1.5 139.569 0.999

Each chain uses 605,000 iterations, discards 205,000 and retains every 200th draw. The first stored draw is omitted and draws are sign-aligned before the diagnostics and pooled summaries. An initial shorter run had lingering drift among several older members, so it was replaced with this longer run and burn-in. The longer run exposed a historical mixing problem rather than resolving it: chain 1 makes a temporary joint excursion among several early members, while chain 2 remains near their other placement. Maximum R-hat is 1.5, so this is not a clean convergence result. A chain-mean correlation near one does not establish member-level agreement.

The stored scores pool both chains, including the excursion; the discrepant draws have not been discarded to make the diagnostics pass. Weiss and Villaraigosa move together, with Smith shifting in the opposite direction. 6 of the 45 members have R-hat above 1.05; among the 24 members shared with the recent-only fit the maximum is 1.018. Hernandez provides a recent-member comparison on its own vertical scale. These traces diagnose the reported fit; no additional start or sensitivity fit was run. Early-member placement remains preliminary. Effective sample sizes computed separately from within-chain autocorrelation do not override the R-hat warning, and neither diagnostic exhaustively searches other modes.

The two analyses have separate normalizations; this comparison checks relative placement of the shared members rather than asserting unchanged numerical units. No rank-correlation statistic is reported.

Election turnovers follow July 1 in the earlier odd-year elections, then December 14, 2020; December 12, 2022; and December 9, 2024. The transition extended the 2015 and 2017 terms, so no 2019 turnover is invented. The initial 2004 window is left-truncated. Windows include interim officeholders with qualifying responses, and all reuse pooled scores.

The canonical affiliation table includes the nine historical reported claims contributed to PR #21, with source notes accompanying each claim. Existing person IDs are unchanged; the claim ledger retires their earlier Unknown entries and records the new affiliations. Zine’s Republican-to-no-party switch is represented as a separate display category rather than collapsed into one static party. The source provides no precise switch date.

DSA and Abundant Housing LA remain separate indicators. Historical absence of a slate is unknown, not non-endorsement. Organizational plot markers are not backdated before the documented windows; pooled markers show ever-documented support. The DSA comparison uses the 2023 and 2024 sitting-group descriptions. AHLA comparison is restricted to the six incoming members in covered 2024 races; within Democrats its two-person outside set shrinks to Jurado alone. Annual AHLA sources mix election stages.

Verification and estimates

Code/56_check_la_expanded.py checks synthetic parser cases and all historical vote cells against action tallies. Root inspected the original cached journal text for a seeded selection of one contested action in each historical year (18 actions), checking dates, rosters and dissent/absence lists; the selection is reproducible with seed 20261008. The source review is bounded, not a statistical accuracy estimate. The original recent-only source checks remain applicable because its cells are reused unchanged.
